key_insight: Oscillating floating planar bodies at an air-water interface experience hydrodynamic resistance that is well captured by oscillatory Stokes boundary-layer theory when the motion is high-frequency and small-amplitude.
engineering_relevance: The frequency-response and startup models provide a practical way to estimate added mass and damping for interfacial devices, which is useful for designing and controlling floating sensors, actuators, and other surface-bound systems.
method: Drive planar interfacial bodies harmonically using magnetic actuation.
Measure steady-state amplitude response and phase lag across frequencies, masses, sizes, and shapes.
Use response data to extract effective added mass and damping, and compare startup transients to a history-integral model.
evidence_signal: The abstract reports experimental measurements over a range of frequencies, masses, sizes, and shapes, with results consistent with boundary-layer theory and transient predictions from a history integral.
watch_item: The theory is stated to hold best in the limit of small interfacial deformation, so stronger amplitudes or larger surface disturbances may reduce accuracy.
paper_title: Hydrodynamic Resistance on Oscillating Planar Interfacial Bodies
